items.title: [Bambu Lab Community Forum - Latest posts] #BehindThePrint 06: The Hidden Angle
items.content_html:
Behind the Scenes of Our Sandtable Creations

Through our Sandtable Exhibition projects, we explore the possibilities of 3D printing by creating detailed miniature worlds that bring together design, engineering, and craftsmanship.

In our #BehindThePrint series, we share the unexpected challenges, creative decisions, and practical lessons behind these creations.

Even the smallest architectural details in our miniature worlds can reveal unexpected 3D-printing challenges.

When the Corners Have Other Ideas

At first glance, there was nothing particularly unusual about the colorful geometric structures in our miniature climbing gym.

The raised details featured sloping edges designed at a 40° overhang angle. For our intended printing conditions, that seemed like a reasonable choice.

And for the most part, the prints looked fine.

Except for the corners.

While the straight edges appeared relatively clean, the corners developed rough, uneven surfaces. The problem was particularly noticeable around the green sections of the model.

The straight edges printed relatively cleanly, but the corners revealed unexpected surface defects

So what was different about those corners?

It looked like insufficient cooling was one factor affecting print quality. But the model’s geometry revealed another important part of the problem.

The corners weren’t actually following the same overhang angle as the edges.

And the difference was bigger than we might expect.

The Angle We Didn’t See

When designing an overhang, we usually pay attention to the angle of the sloping surface. If it falls within a range our printer can comfortably handle, the design should be reasonably printable.

Or so it seems.

The tricky part is that, on shapes with sharp corners, the angle we design along an edge isn’t necessarily the steepest angle the printer encounters.

Imagine a square column with a sloping section that gradually widens as it rises.

With every new layer, the edges extend slightly farther outward. Along a straight edge, this movement follows the intended 40° slope.

But something different happens at the corners.

Here, two edges meet, and their outward extensions combine diagonally. That means each corner reaches farther beyond the previous layer than the straight edges do.

Only a little farther, at first glance. But enough to change the effective overhang angle significantly.

The corner extends farther outward than the straight edge, creating a steeper effective overhang between successive layers.

For our four-sided shape, the numbers reveal just how much this matters.

The straight edges were designed at 40°.

At the corners, however, the effective overhang angle reached approximately 49.9°.

That’s almost 10° steeper than the original design angle!

For this production case, we were working with a maximum overhang target of 45°, allowing a margin for less favorable printing conditions.

The straight edges were within that target. The corners had quietly crossed it.

Suddenly, those rough corners made much more sense.

What Happens When We Change the Shape?

The interesting thing about this problem is that we don’t necessarily need to change the printer settings to address it.

Sometimes, we can make geometry work in our favor. And there are several ways to approach it.

More Sides, Less Trouble

What if our square shape wasn’t quite so square?

Imagine replacing the four-sided prism with one that has eight sides. The top-down shape becomes a little closer to a circle, and its corners become less pronounced.

That also changes how far those corners extend beyond the previous layer.

With the same 40° edge angle, the calculated maximum corner angle drops from approximately 49.9° to just 42.2°.

Adding more sides brings the effective corner overhang closer to the intended 40° edge angle.

The columns with multiple sides never faced the printing issues like the 4 sided version did

Of course, adding sides changes the appearance of the model. If a sharp, square shape is essential to the design, this might not be the ideal solution.

Fortunately, it isn’t the only option.

A Gentler Slope

Another approach is to keep the four-sided shape but reduce its straight edge angle.

For example, changing the edge angle from 40° to 35° reduces the calculated corner angle to approximately 44.7°.

That brings even the corners within our 45° design target.

It’s a relatively straightforward geometric adjustment, although the gentler slope also changes the proportions of the feature.

A gentler slope reduces the effective overhang angle at the corners without changing the number of sides.

Or Simply Soften the Corners

There’s also a third possibility: rounding the corners themselves.

Instead of allowing two straight edges to meet at a sharp point, we can introduce a curved transition.

This reduces the pronounced diagonal extension at the corner and can bring the maximum overhang closer to the intended edge angle.

Rounded corners reduce the abrupt change in geometry responsible for the steeper corner overhang.

Which approach makes the most sense depends on the design.

Sometimes we can change the overall shape. Other times, preserving its appearance matters more.

The important thing is understanding what the geometry is doing before deciding how to improve it.

By this point, you probably wonder about all these nice diagrams and calculations shared above. We have this handy little tool as a download link for you.

Feel free to check it out and explore how the straight slope or corner count will affect the corner angle.

A Different Way to Look at Overhangs

Our miniature climbing-gym component highlights a detail that’s surprisingly easy to overlook.

When we check an overhang, we’re often looking at the most obvious sloping surface. But the printer doesn’t only have to deal with that surface. It also has to build the corners where those surfaces meet.

And as we’ve seen, those corners can behave quite differently.

This doesn’t mean every sharp corner will cause printing problems. Actual print quality also depends on cooling, material, speed, and other conditions.

But it does give us another useful consideration when designing parts with overhangs: check the most demanding part of the geometry, not just the angle that’s easiest to see.

Sometimes, the trickiest overhang isn’t on the surface we’re looking at. It’s hiding right around the corner.

More Stories Behind the Print

From unexpected layer lines to hidden geometric challenges, our Sandtable projects keep reminding us that small design details can make a big difference.

Have you ever encountered a print that looked perfectly reasonable in the model but turned out differently than expected?

We’d love to hear what you discovered.

See you in the next #BehindThePrint!

items.title: [smarthomeassistent.de] Nginx vulnerabilities threaten smart home systems; Frigate releases emergency update
items.content_html: The developers of the open-source network video recorder Frigate released version 0.18.3 on November 19, which fixes a critical vulnerability in the bundled nginx web server. nginx 1.27.4 was affected: with HTTP/2 enabled, attackers could execute code without authentication via an accessible Frigate web server. Frigate’s developers describe the flaw as a vulnerability that allows code execution with root privileges; according to security researchers, however, escalating from the nginx process to root privileges on the host also requires a Linux kernel vulnerability. The vulnerability is one of ten security flaws that manufacturer F5 fixed with an nginx update released on November 18. F5 rates five of them 9.2 out of 10 under CVSS 4.0. According to security researchers, two HTTP/2 flaws allow remote attacks without authentication. Frigate 0.18.3 updates nginx to version 1.30.7 and also restricts certain options in the go2rtc camera-streaming component. The update is particularly urgent for operators who have made Frigate’s web interface accessible over the internet; the security advisories list ports 5000 and 8971. Installations accessible only on the home network should also be updated, as a compromised device could serve as an entry point. Frigate recommends backing up the configuration and database before updating. For standalone nginx installations, the security advisories list version 1.30.7 for the stable branch and 1.31.9 for the mainline branch as the fixed releases.

items.content_html:
This notification, just dropped - are Makerworld listening???

MakerWorld Community Guidelines Update

2026-11-19 03:58

Hi MakerWorld Community,

We are updating the rules for model images, focusing on improving their authenticity and consistency with the actual models, in order to continuously enhance the quality of content and the user experience within the community.

This update includes three core changes:

  1. The cover image must show the complete model, match the model files, and accurately reflect the finished 3D print.
  2. The cover image must match the structure, material appearance, and color regions shown in real printed images .
  3. When uploading a model, you must provide at least three photos of the actual 3D print from different angles, in addition to the cover image. These photos must match the model files.

We are also reminding you to follow the existing image rules for Print Profiles.

Detailed rules, examples, execution specifics, and important considerations have been provided in the community announcement.

Click here to view the full announcement

Thank you for your understanding and cooperation as we work together to create a more trustworthy creative environment.

MakerWorld Team

items.title: [smarthomeassistent.de] Home Assistant updates locally integrate HomePod sensors and other smart home devices
items.content_html: Three new or expanded integrations provide additional sensor data for Home Assistant: the community integration HomePod Sensor Link reads temperature and humidity directly from Apple speakers, an update to the X-Sense SBS50 base station expands the integration of compatible security devices, and a new community project integrates EnOcean multisensors via Bluetooth. HomePod Sensor Link has been available in the Home Assistant marketplace since November 16. However, setup requires exported HomeKit keys and changes to macOS security features. X-Sense is rolling out firmware 1.8.7 gradually; after the update, the connection can be configured in the app. The EnOcean integration supports temperature, brightness, motion, and vibration, among other features.

items.content_html: Comparative tests of smart radiator thermostats reveal significant differences in operation, system requirements, and additional costs. In IMTEST’s comparison of ten devices priced between 30 and 100 euros, the Homematic IP Evo radiator thermostat came out on top; according to IMTEST, it also offers geo-fencing and hydraulic balancing without a subscription. The least expensive model tested, the TP-Link Kasa KE100, costs 29.90 euros per thermostat but showed weaknesses in window detection and geo-fencing. In another comparison, the Aqara W600 and the Bosch Radiator Thermostat 2 [+M] each received a score of 1.4; both require a hub. The Shelly TRV, which connects directly to Wi-Fi, received a score of 2.6. Compatibility depends, among other things, on the valve connection and the hub already in place; some features incur subscription fees.

items.title: [Bambu Lab Community Forum - Latest posts] X2D – Improve the left PTFE connector with a screw-locking compression fitting
items.content_html:
Alama:

In the meantime, I’m currently designing a 3D-printable solution that could help prevent the PTFE tube from tearing.

Are you working on a solution different than the PTFE tube guides that are already available on Makerworld? My feeling is that the tube guide along with a riser should substantially reduce this issue. I went 500 hours with just a riser, and when I examined the main extruder tube, it had some gouges from the teeth in the fitting, but it was still largely intact. With the guide installed, I’m sure it will be less.

My primary concern at this point is the PTFE tube twisting in the fitting as the head moves to different locations. This will also cause the teeth on the fitting to gouge the tube. A clamp on tube guide would be needed to keep the tube from twisting, but a clamp might constrict the tube and cause filament drag.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] The ‘recession indicators’ visible at your workplace
items.content_html:
People all over the U.S. have been sharing their “personal recession indicators” in recent months, from only being able to afford Goldfish crackers and water for lunch to filling up their cars with a few dollars’ worth of gas at a time.

According to employment attorney Craig Levey, a partner at Bennett & Belfort, there are recession indicators at your workplace, too—you just have to take a look around. And they could be a sign that bigger cutbacks, or even layoffs, could be around the corner.

Levey makes content on TikTok, where he tracks patterns in his comments and feed that highlight how people feel about the world of work.

“Over the last few months, I noticed that a lot of companies were suffering financial issues. There was a downturn in their numbers,” he tells Fast Company. “People were trying to assess whether a recession was happening in the United States.”

Levey posted a video about workplace recession indicators that employees should look out for, including companies slashing expenses on business trips, bonuses, holiday parties, and even office snacks. Companies often start with the little things when tightening their belts, he says, and these cuts could be an early signal that a business is preparing for tougher economic conditions.

“Upper management and leadership, they probably get together and they say, ‘Okay, we need to cut costs. What can we do? Let’s cut the low-hanging fruit,’” he says.

Cutting now to save later

Companies do this, Levey says, because they’re looking six, 12, or even 18 months ahead, and taking preemptive steps to put themselves in a better position for the next fiscal year.

These cuts may seem trivial to some. But for other employees, they can be incredibly important. Levey says he regularly hears from people who have full-time jobs but have to live in their cars because they can no longer afford rent.

“A lot of employees are really struggling because the day-to-day costs are so high that they can’t pay their bills,” Levey says. “If you’re somebody who can’t pay their rent, trying to figure out how you’re going to get your next meal, and you can go into your company’s kitchen and get a snack—that makes a big difference.”

According to Chris Marvel Davis, cofounder of Pivot, a training and development provider that runs workshops on wellness, burnout, and leadership, snacks may be what people notice first. But there are other, less obvious signs that a company is becoming more cautious with its spending. 

Travel and conference requests getting denied or delayed may not be immediately apparent, he tells Fast Company. Other signs include open roles staying unfilled, job postings disappearing, backfills for departed employees being paused, and contractors being let go before full-time employees.

“Small purchases need bigger approvals,” he adds. “When a $200 expense suddenly needs a director’s sign-off, someone in finance is watching cash closely.”

Is it routine or a sign of something bigger?

Companies make these kinds of cuts first because they’re easier to reverse, Davis says. On their own, they may simply suggest that leadership is being careful.

“They buy leadership time to see how bad things might get without alarming employees or customers,” he says. “One sign by itself doesn’t tell you much, but several at once are worth taking seriously.”

People should also pay attention to what happens the next time someone leaves, Chiquita Hall-Jackson, an employment attorney at Hall-Jackson & Associates, tells Fast Company.

“If the company leaves the position vacant, divides the work among the remaining team, and still expects the same output, that tells you more about its staffing plans than a cut to the travel budget,” she says. “When that pattern shows up across teams, it’s worth asking whether leadership is planning to operate with fewer people.”

According to Hall-Jackson, it’s also a good idea to look at what’s being cut and how long the cuts last. A canceled off-site meeting may save money once, but a hiring freeze changes how the business operates.

“One budget decision can have plenty of explanations,” she says. “Several decisions that consistently reduce staffing or hours are more meaningful.”

Another potential warning sign is a change in the company’s management structure. If there are fewer middle managers than there used to be, and larger teams are now reporting to more senior supervisors, that could suggest the company is looking to operate with fewer people, Levey says.

It’s more important than ever to have leverage

Of course, many of these signs could just mean that an individual company isn’t doing well and may not indicate a wider, looming recession. 

But in this tough economy and job market, employees should consider being more sensitive to changes at work that may hint at something bigger happening, Levey says. He adds that it’s important to maintain a sense of where you stand within the company, how secure your position is, and what the general temperature is when it comes to potential layoffs.

“You want to pay attention to messages from the CEO or upper management. Because if you think that your job is in jeopardy, then while you’re still employed there and making a wage, you’ve got to start looking elsewhere to see what your other options are,” Levey says.

The worst thing is being blindsided, so it’s always a good idea to make sure you have some leverage, he notes. “It doesn’t mean you need to microanalyze every single thing that happens with the company. But be a realist. Keep your eyes open, really understand what’s going on. That way, you’re less surprised if these things happen.”

items.title: [Dreaming3D Inc - News] From a Napkin Sketch to a Printable File
items.content_html:
&&&

From a Napkin Sketch to a Printable File: How We Turn Ideas Into 3D Models in San Diego

You don't need a file to get something 3D printed. You need an idea and a few numbers. Here's how we turn sketches, photos and old parts into models that fit on the first real print.

By Dreaming3D in Carmel Valley, San Diego. November 15, 2026.

Most people who text us about a print don't have a file. They have a drawing on the back of a receipt, a photo of the thing that snapped, a knob off a 1990s stereo, or just a sentence: “I need something that holds this to that.” That's a fine place to start. A 3D printer can't print an idea, though. It prints a file, and somebody has to make that file. In our shop, that's the job this post is about.

The short version

  • Bring whatever you have: a description, a sketch, a photo with a coin in it, someone else's drawing, or the part itself.
  • We model it in parametric CAD, design it for the printer that will make it, test-print anything that has to fit, then print the real part.
  • Design time is quoted before we start. Printing is $7 an hour of machine time on FDM and $9 on resin, plus material.
  • Ask for the files and they come with the part: STL or 3MF to print, STEP to edit.
  • We don't make weapon parts, flight hardware, safety-critical parts or patient-contact medical devices, and we don't copy other people's art or brands.

What you can bring us, and what each one tells us

Every starting point carries some information and leaves some out. None of them is wrong. The table is just so you know what we'll ask next.

What you have What it tells us What's still missing What helps most
An idea in words What the part has to do The shape and every size Measurements of whatever it attaches to, and where it will live
A sketch or drawing The shape you have in mind Real sizes, unless you wrote them on Write the numbers you know on the drawing, and mark which ones must match something
A photo Shape and proportions Scale and depth A quarter or a ruler lying in the same plane, camera straight on, plus one side view
A dimensioned drawing or someone else's CAD file Nearly everything Print-specific details The original file (STEP, PDF, DXF), not a screenshot of it
The physical part, even broken The real geometry Missing pieces and hidden insides All the pieces, plus whatever it mates with
Concept art or reference images The look The third dimension A front view and a side view, and the size you want it

The most useful thing you can send is a measurement of whatever the part has to fit. A cable clip can be any shape you like; the diameter of the cable can't. If you only measure one thing, measure that.

The quarter trick for photos

A US quarter is 24.26 mm across (U.S. Mint specification). Lay one flat next to the object, in the same plane, and shoot from straight above. The coin gives us the scale for the outline. It won't rescue a photo taken at an angle, because the lens shrinks whatever is farther away, and it tells us nothing about depth. That's why a second photo from the side helps, and why anything that has to fit still gets measured.

How an idea becomes a printable file

This is the order we work in, whether the job is a single replacement knob or a run of custom cable organizers for a small business.

  1. Talk through what it has to do

    Function before shape: what it holds, what it touches, how it gets used, where it lives (a kitchen drawer, a car, a boat slip in Mission Bay), and how many you need. This decides the material and the printer before anyone opens a CAD program.

  2. Pin down the numbers that matter

    Calipers on the parts it has to fit, a photo with a coin for the outline, or a scan for complex surfaces. Our scanner is a Revopoint MetroY; Revopoint rates it at up to 0.02 mm single-frame accuracy. That's the maker's figure, and it isn't certified metrology.

  3. Model it in parametric CAD

    Every dimension is a number we can change later, so “make it 2 mm taller” is a quick edit, not a redraw. Organic shapes like a figurine or a sculpted handle get sculpted instead, which trades editable numbers for freedom of form.

  4. Design it for the printer

    Choose the print orientation, keep overhangs at 45° or less where we can, size walls, holes and clearances for the machine and material, and split anything bigger than the build plate.

  5. Print the risky part first

    If something has to fit, we print just that feature first: the hole, the clip, the slot. A small test piece costs minutes of machine time; a wrong full print costs hours.

  6. Revise, then print the real one

    Adjust the model from the test, print the final part in the right material, and hand it over with the files if you want them.

Step 2 is where most of the accuracy comes from, and step 5 is where most of the money is saved. If you'd rather learn to do steps 3 and 4 yourself, that's what our tutoring lesson plan covers, from Tinkercad to Fusion.

Designing for the printer: the part nobody sees

A model can look perfect on screen and still print badly. An FDM printer builds a part as a stack of thin layers, and every layer needs something under it. So the same shape can be easy or awkward to print depending on which way up it goes. Here is our example knob both ways.

Printed the way it's installed, the knob has a flat ledge under the cap: a 90° overhang that needs supports, and supports leave marks right where your fingers go. Flipped cap down, nothing is steeper than 45°, so it prints with no supports at all. That flip also changes a smaller detail: stem down, the blind end of the screw hole would be a 4.5 mm bridge, just under the 5 mm span that Protolabs Network (formerly Hubs) says prints without sag. Cap down, the hole opens upward and there's no bridge.

The sketch had a rounded top edge. In the model it became a 45° chamfer. Protolabs Network suggests a chamfer or a radius on edges that touch the plate, to hide the slight first-layer flare called elephant's foot. We picked the chamfer because at 45° it also stays inside the overhang limit. That's the kind of decision you never see in the finished part, and it's most of what design for printing is.

The rules of thumb we check, and where they come from

Feature Rule of thumb Source
Overhangs Up to 45° from vertical usually prints without support; steeper needs support Protolabs Network (Hubs)
Bridges Some sag or support marks unless the span is under 5 mm Protolabs Network (Hubs)
Small pins Under 5 mm across may print as outline only, which makes a weak joint; add a fillet at the base Protolabs Network (Hubs)
Vertical holes Often print undersized; for critical holes, print small and drill to size Protolabs Network (Hubs)
Edges on the plate A 45° chamfer or a radius hides the first-layer flare called elephant's foot Protolabs Network (Hubs)
Clearance between parts 0.5 mm for FDM and resin on simple shapes (JLC3DP); 0.015 in, about 0.38 mm, in XY on Stratasys Direct's FDM machines JLC3DP; Stratasys Direct
FDM wall thickness 1.6 mm on a 50 × 50 mm part, 2.0 mm at 100 × 100 mm, 2.5 mm at 200 × 200 mm JLC3DP
Strength Parts are weaker across the layers than along them, so orientation follows the load Protolabs Network (Hubs)

Notice that the two clearance figures don't agree. That's normal: clearance depends on the printer, the material and the settings. Published numbers are a starting point, which is why anything that has to slide, snap or press-fit gets a small test print on the machine that will make the real part.

How big can one piece be?

Printer Type Build volume Good for Source
Bambu Lab A1 FDM 256 × 256 × 256 mm Most functional parts Bambu spec sheet
Creality CR-10S FDM 300 × 300 × 400 mm Tall or large parts CR-10 series spec
Elegoo Saturn 4 Ultra 16K Resin 211.68 × 118.37 × 220 mm Fine detail: 14 × 19 µm XY pixels, per Elegoo Elegoo

Anything bigger gets split into pieces that fit, with the joints designed into the model so they line up when assembled.

Replicas: when the original exists

If you already have the thing, or what's left of it, we start from the real geometry. Simple shapes we measure with calipers. Complex curves we scan. A scan is a dense mesh of points, not a model, so we rebuild it as clean CAD and use the scan to check our work. Missing chunks get rebuilt from symmetry and from whatever the part mates with, the way the hero knob above gets its rim back.

The full scan-to-print process, with what scanning can and can't do, is in our reverse engineering guide. If you want to know why we keep scanning, modeling and printing under one roof, this post explains it.

What we will and won’t copy

We'll replicate functional parts for things you own: a knob, a clip, a battery cover, a trim piece. We won't copy someone else's sculpture, character, logo or branded product. If you plan to sell copies of anything, talk to an intellectual property attorney first. We're a print shop, not lawyers.

“Can’t AI just turn my drawing into a file?”

The pitch: “AI can turn any doodle into a printable part in minutes.”

Free sketch-to-3D tools such as PrintPal really do turn a drawing into an STL in minutes, with no modeling experience. For a figurine, an ornament or a concept to hold in your hand, that's genuinely useful.

What gets left out: a picture carries no measurements, and the mesh that comes back has no dimensions you can edit. Even a company that sells AI generation, Neural4D, writes that AI is strongest for organic and decorative forms, and that a part which must fit an existing object within 0.2 mm is still faster to build in CAD.

Our rule is simple. If it only has to look right, an AI mesh can be a fine starting point, and we'll repair and size it for printing. If it clips, screws, slides or replaces something, it gets modeled in CAD with real numbers.

The files you get

Format What's inside Use it for
STL Triangles only. No units, no color, no print settings. Printing on any slicer and any printer
3MF Geometry plus units, color, several objects on one plate, and often the slicer settings. An open standard from the 3MF Consortium. Reprinting with the settings we tuned (Bambu Studio, PrusaSlicer, OrcaSlicer)
STEP The exact CAD geometry, so curves stay curves. The standard way to move a model between CAD programs. Editing the design later in another CAD program, or sending it to a machine shop

One trap worth knowing: an STL has no units (SimplyPrint, 3Dnatives). A part exported in inches and opened as millimeters comes in 25.4 times too small. A 3MF stores its units, which is one reason we prefer it for anything you'll reprint.

Material is part of the design, San Diego edition

Where the part lives changes how we model it, because it changes what we print it in.

  • Indoors at room temperature: PLA is usually fine, and it's the easiest material to print accurately.
  • In a car: Bambu's data sheet puts PLA Basic's heat deflection temperature at 57 °C (0.45 MPa test). In a 2018 study by Arizona State and the UC San Diego School of Medicine, dashboards in sun-parked cars averaged 157 °F, about 69 °C, after an hour (ASU). Those were Tempe days in the 100s, not a marine-layer morning in Del Mar, but an inland August afternoon gets closer than you'd think. Car parts get a higher-temperature material like ASA or ABS.
  • Outside near the coast: sun and salt air. We print in UV-resistant ASA and design in stainless hardware rather than plain steel screws.
  • Small and detailed: miniatures, jewelry masters and small raised text go to resin, which holds detail FDM can't.
  • Bendy: grips, bumpers and gaskets get TPU, which changes the design too, since flexible parts need thicker walls to hold their shape.

If you're not sure whether your part wants FDM or resin, our FDM vs SLA vs SLS guide walks through the trade-offs.

What we won’t make

Being clear about this up front saves everyone time:

  • Firearm components or other weapon parts
  • Flight hardware
  • Load-bearing or safety-critical parts, meaning anything whose failure could hurt someone
  • Medical devices that touch a patient
  • Metal parts (we print plastic and resin)
  • Copies of someone else's sculpture, character, logo or branded product

If you're not sure which side of the line your idea falls on, ask. We'd rather have the conversation than guess.

What it costs and how long it takes

Design time is quoted up front, after we've seen what you have. A spacer or a knob takes far less modeling than a multi-part enclosure, and we'll tell you which you're looking at before you pay anything. Printing is billed by machine time: $7 an hour on FDM and $9 an hour on resin, plus material.

Most of the calendar time on a design job goes to test prints and your feedback, not to the modeling itself. You don't need to be local for any of it: photos, measurements and approvals work fine over text and email, and we can look at the problem together on a video call.

Questions people ask before sending an idea

Do I need to know CAD to work with you?

No. Most people who bring us an idea have never opened a CAD program. A clear description, a few measurements and a photo or sketch are enough to start. If you'd rather learn to model it yourself, we tutor that too, starting with Tinkercad and moving to Fusion.

What should I send along with a sketch?

The numbers you know, written right on the drawing, even rough ones. Then tell us which sizes have to match something real, like a pipe, a screw or a shelf edge, and which ones are just about looks. A photo of where the part will go helps more than people expect.

Can you make a 3D model from a photo?

Yes, for the shape. Put a US quarter flat next to the object, in the same plane, and shoot from straight above; the quarter is 24.26 mm across, so it gives us the scale. Anything that has to fit still gets measured with calipers, because a photo bends with the lens and hides depth.

Can you copy a part I already have?

Yes, if it's a functional part for something you own, like a broken knob, a clip or a cover. Simple parts we measure with calipers; complex ones we scan, then rebuild as a clean model. We don't copy someone else's sculpture, character, logo or branded product.

Do I get the 3D file?

Ask and we'll send the files with your part: STL or 3MF to print it again, and STEP if you want to edit the design in another CAD program later.

Can you work from an AI-generated model?

Yes. AI sketch-to-3D tools are good at decorative shapes. Send us the mesh and we'll repair it, size it and make it printable. If it has to fit something, we'll usually rebuild the fitting features in CAD.

How accurate will the printed part be?

It depends on the printer, the material and the feature, which is why we test-print anything that has to fit before the final print. For fine detail like miniatures or small text, resin on our Saturn 4 Ultra 16K is the better choice than FDM.

What if my idea is bigger than your printers?

We split it into pieces that fit, design the joints into the model, and assemble them. The largest single piece we can print is 300 × 300 × 400 mm on our CR-10S.

Do I have to be in San Diego?

No. Design work happens over text, email and video calls, and we ship finished parts. Being local helps when we need to measure the thing your part attaches to, and San Diego County customers can hand us the part in person.

Send us what you’ve got

A photo of the sketch, the broken part, or the spot where the thing needs to go is enough to start. We'll reply with questions, then a quote.

Send us your idea

Or text a photo to 858-342-6984, email dreaming3dprinting@gmail.com, or message @dreaming3dprinting on Instagram. Our shop is in Carmel Valley and serves all of San Diego County; finished parts ship anywhere.

Your turn: what's the thing you've been meaning to get made but never had a file for? Tell us in the comments, or tag us on Instagram.

Update-

I’d been talking with Bambu Lab about exchanging my H3C, but I didn’t hear back for a few days. I left for vacation today and can’t ship it back until I return on 12/1, so I’ve ordered replacement idler pulleys to start the repair myself. They should be waiting for me when I get home. If only I’d had a little more patience! Seeing that the H3C is backordered until 12/11 made the decision easier. Now I just need to get my hands on some TPU 75A and a few 0.2 mm hotends.
